To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) by using a combination of data from an expert’s demonstrations and data collected from an agent’s own interactions with the environment, we can solve sequential decision-making problems more effectively, and (2) we can solve such problems in an efficient way using a policy improvement algorithm based on convex optimization.

we propose an algorithm for sequential decision making problems that utilizes two data sources: an agent interacts sequentially with the environment to obtain a set of data samples, and an expert provides a set of demonstrations, and we prove that this algorithm converges to a locally optimal policy.

(1) we propose a novel algorithm to solve uncertain Markov decision processes that utilizes two different sources of data, (2) the algorithm is formulated in the Approximate Policy Iterations framework, and (3) the algorithm outperformed other methods in a real robotic navigation problem.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we provide a novel framework to solve sequential decision-making problems by combining reinforcement learning and supervised learning, and we demonstrate that the framework works effectively in real-world applications.
we propose an algorithm to learn a policy from a mixture of data sources, and demonstrate its effectiveness on a challenging robotic navigation task.

we propose an algorithm that utilizes the data sources available in real world applications, which are not available to pure approximate policy iteration, to solve sequential decision-making problems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expert demonstrations can be used to improve the learning process in reinforcement learning tasks.
the algorithm can learn to perform well in a real task even when the agent is provided with only 10 expert demonstrations and a few thousand data points from the environment.
the use of expert demonstration data can significantly enhance the performance of the agent in sequential decision-making tasks.
